analysis.one_liner: Bases Medicare drug coinsurance on the discounted net price of a drug, not its inflated list price.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2024 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025 without a single vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare Part D plans often charge seniors a percentage of a drug's "list price" even though the plans actually pay a lower "net price" after rebates and discounts from drugmakers. This bill would require that coinsurance be calculated from the lower net price, so seniors' out-of-pocket drug costs would reflect what the drug really costs. It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors with Medicare Part D who pay percentage-based coinsurance on their prescriptions. When a drug's list price is higher than the net price the plan actually pays after rebates, those seniors would pay coinsurance on the lower, real-world price, lowering their out-of-pocket drug costs.

how_it_helps.text: It amends Medicare Part D law to require that, for plan years starting January 1, 2025, any coinsurance on a covered Part D drug be calculated from the drug's net price — the negotiated price after manufacturer discounts and rebates — rather than the higher list price.

It defines net price using the manufacturer price concessions reported by plans in the Detailed DIR Report, so the discount drugmakers give the system would actually flow through to seniors' out-of-pocket costs.
The rule applies to the cost-sharing band between the annual deductible and the out-of-pocket threshold, the range where most seniors pay percentage-based coinsurance.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare drug plans and pharmacy benefit managers would collect less in coinsurance, and brand-name drugmakers would see their discounts reflected in what seniors pay rather than absorbed by the system; plan premiums could rise slightly to cover the difference.

drawbacks.text: The bill only applies to drugs subject to coinsurance rather than flat copayments, and excludes certain drugs under paragraphs (8) and (9) of the statutory scheme, so many Medicare Part D beneficiaries would see no change in their out-of-pocket costs.

Because coinsurance percentages applied to lower net prices would generate less revenue for plans, insurers and pharmacy benefit managers could seek to recoup the difference through higher premiums or copays, and the bill does not prohibit that.
The net price calculation depends on plans' own annual reporting (the Detailed DIR Report), so accuracy hinges on plan self-reporting with no independent audit mechanism in the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea is sound and low-cost: charging seniors coinsurance on the discounted price is a straightforward consumer protection. The main tradeoff is administrative — plans would need to report net prices accurately — and the cost of any revenue reduction would fall on Medicare plans and, indirectly, drug manufacturers rather than on seniors. The bill's fatal weakness was not design but attention: with one Republican cosponsor and a Senate split narrowly, it had little path.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up, so it expired without any vote when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Jacky Rosen introduced S. 4229 on May 1, 2024, with Republican Sen. John Cornyn as an original cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance — the committee with jurisdiction over Medicare.
No further action was ever taken; the Finance Committee held no markup and the Senate never voted on it.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, meaning it would have to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and pharmacy benefit managers keep collecting coinsurance on inflated list prices, and drugmakers' rebates stay buried in plan finances rather than reaching seniors.

for.name: Sen. John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as the lone Republican supporter.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the referred bill — no markup, no report, no vote — during the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had one Senate Republican cosponsor (1 of 49) among a Democratic sponsor, but the Finance Committee never acted, so no party split was ever tested on a vote.

industries.note: Manufacturers would effectively have to pass their rebate savings through to beneficiaries rather than letting plans charge coinsurance on the inflated list price. Their interest ran against the bill's benefit to seniors.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plans and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: Plans would owe more accurate reporting of net prices and could see lower cost-sharing revenue; the bill does not bar them from recouping through premiums. Their gatekeeping role over drug pricing is untouched.
